meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Stay hungry, stay foolish'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Steve Jobs — it was Stewart Brand’s sign-off on the last Whole Earth Catalog (1974). Jobs quoted and credited it at Stanford in 2005.

answer.label: Not Steve Jobs — actually Stewart Brand
answer.authorDates: b. 14 December 1938 · American writer and editor; creator of the Whole Earth Catalog
answer.sourceLine: The words were the farewell sign-off Brand wrote on the back cover of the Whole Earth Epilog (October 1974), beneath a photo of an early-morning country road. Steve Jobs quoted it — and explicitly credited it to Brand — in his 2005 Stanford commencement address, which is why it is now popularly pinned on Jobs.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
trail: The four words were the sign-off on the back cover of the Whole Earth Epilog, the final issue of Stewart Brand’s catalog, in October 1974.
Steve Jobs recited them — naming Brand and the catalog — at the close of his 2005 Stanford commencement speech, seeding the modern misattribution.
Brand has said he meant the free, slightly hungry, faintly foolish mindset of a young hitchhiker at dawn.
source.excerptNote: On the back cover of the final Whole Earth Catalog was a photograph of an early-morning country road — the kind you might hitchhike on — and beneath it these four words, as the editors signed off for good. Brand later explained he had in mind the frame of mind of a young hitchhiker at dawn: “You’re always a little bit hungry and you know you are being completely foolish.”

author.name: Stewart Brand
author.heading: Who was Stewart Brand?
author.metaLine: b. 1938 · writer, editor and founder of the Whole Earth Catalog
author.bio: Stewart Brand (born 1938) is an American writer, editor and entrepreneur who launched the Whole Earth Catalog in 1968 as a countercultural “access to tools” guide for self-sufficient living. He edited its various editions and wrote the farewell message on the back cover of the final issue in 1974. Brand went on to co-found The WELL online community and the Long Now Foundation, and remains an influential figure in technology and environmental thought.

misattribution.heading: Why people credit Steve Jobs
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most-quoted things Steve Jobs ever said — but he was quoting someone else, and said so plainly.

items.why: Jobs made the phrase famous by ending his 2005 Stanford commencement address with it, but in the same breath he credited “a fellow named Stewart Brand” and the Whole Earth Catalog. He did not originate it.

misattribution.truthLine: The four words were Stewart Brand’s farewell sign-off on the back cover of the final Whole Earth Catalog in 1974 — Jobs popularized them, but the words are Brand’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Whole Earth Catalog was, in Jobs’s words, “one of the bibles of my generation” — a pre-internet compendium of tools and ideas for building a self-directed life. Its 1974 sign-off distilled that ethos into four words about staying curious, restless and willing to look foolish in pursuit of something interesting.
detailsBody: Brand has explained the image behind the line: a young hitchhiker on a country road at dawn, in one of the freest frames of mind there is — a little hungry, and knowingly a little foolish. Jobs adopted it as a personal mantra and passed it to the Stanford class of 2005, giving Brand’s farewell a second, far larger life.
